newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: INTERVIEW - JP Morgan homes in on S.Africa.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - JP Morgan homes in on S.Africa.

text.p: U.S. investment bank JP Morgan & Co Inc, already a major player in South African debt and the rand, plans to double its trading capacity after moving dealing operations from London to Johannesburg in June.
The company, which last month joined the South African Futures Exchange (Safex), is about to apply for membership of the Bond Exchange and may join the Johannesburg Stock Exchange at a later date.
Ronald Gault, head of the company's South African office which opened last October, also has his eye firmly on new corporate finance business, including advising on upcoming privatisations.
"Our plan is to become a full service branch bank," he said in an interview, adding he hoped to receive a banking licence from the Reserve Bank within six to eight months.

Gault expects growth in South Africa's financial markets to accelerate as investors gain confidence in the African National Congress government, and its ability to deliver both disciplined economics and market liberalisation. Easing of exchange controls would also stimulate business, he said.
"There is a sense of stability now in South Africa that investors want to see and which they consider to be very important."

Andrew McDougall, who will head up the Johannesburg dealing operation, said JP Morgan would have a dealing staff of around 20 in Johannesburg of whom some 12 will be traders, four sales people and the balance research and support staff. There are currently six South African traders in London.
"We're basically doubling our overall trading capacity," McDougall said by telephone from London.

JP Morgan is best known in South Africa's foreign exchange and fixed income markets, where it has gained a reputation as a powerful player. But McDougall said it was also focusing on equity derivatives on Safex, which deals almost exclusively in stock index futures and options.
Further down the line, the firm hopes to be a market-maker in South African government rand bonds as the authorities move to transfer market-making from the Reserve Bank to private institutions.
"We have a predisposition and a capacity to be a market-maker," Gault said.

On the banking side of the business, where JP Morgan has an established track record in raising capital for South African borrowers, Gault said it intended to build on a fairly broad book of business already in place with leading corporates, and would seek opportunities in black empowerment deals.
"We are also going to focus very sharply on government business...We're very excited by privatisation and you can expect that we will be pitching for business," he said.
The upcoming sale of part or all of South African Airways SAA.CN was one contract likely to interest the firm.
JP Morgan made unsuccessful bids on both the buy and sell side for the recent $1.26 billion privatisation of a 30 percent stake in Telkom.
